title: Clearing Up "New Testament Only" and Other Common Mix-Ups
summary: Closing this section on denominational nuance by clearing up a handful of common, easy-to-make mix-ups reverts and their families run into.

body.text: A grab-bag of common mix-ups, cleared up directly

Closing out this section on denominational nuance: a handful of specific, common mix-ups reverts and their Christian family members tend to make when discussing these two faiths — quick, direct clarifications worth having ready.
Mix-up 1: "Islam is like a stricter version of the Old Testament"

While the earlier lesson on Old Testament law and Sharia found real structural parallels, Islam isn't simply "more Old Testament" than Christianity — it has its own distinct scripture, theology, and prophet, not a repackaging of Judaism. The parallel is structural and worth knowing, but shouldn't be overstated into an actual genealogical claim.
Mix-up 2: "Muslims don't believe in the Bible at all"

As covered earlier in this collection, Islam teaches belief in the earlier scriptures given by God, including material Christians recognise, even while holding the tahrif doctrine about their transmission over time — "don't believe in the Bible at all" isn't an accurate summary of the Islamic position.
Mix-up 3: "Sunni and Shia are basically like Catholic and Protestant"

This comparison is sometimes offered as a quick explainer, but it's not a close match — the Sunni-Shia split originated over a political and leadership succession dispute after the Prophet's death, not primarily over the kind of doctrinal disagreements (justification, sacraments, biblical authority) that split Catholic and Protestant Christianity. Real theological differences did develop between Sunni and Shia Islam over the centuries, but the origin and structure of the split differs enough that the comparison, while intuitive, can be more misleading than clarifying if taken too literally.
Mix-up 4: "Reverting to Islam means rejecting the Old Testament and New Testament entirely"

As covered throughout this collection, Islam holds a nuanced position — respect for earlier scripture as originally revealed, alongside the belief that its transmission was altered over time and that the Quran is the final, corrected, and complete revelation. "Rejecting the Bible entirely" oversimplifies a more layered position.

body.question: Are there other common mix-ups worth knowing about?
body.answer: Yes, many — this lesson covers a representative sample rather than an exhaustive list; if you encounter a specific mix-up repeatedly with your own family, it's worth researching that specific point carefully (using this app's AI Mentor or a knowledgeable local scholar) so you can address it accurately and confidently.

body.question: What's the best general approach when family makes one of these mix-ups?
body.answer: Gently clarifying with specifics, rather than simply saying "that's wrong," tends to work best — for instance, explaining precisely what Islam does teach about the Bible, rather than just correcting the phrase "Muslims don't believe in the Bible at all" without offering the more accurate version.
